question_en: Credit card receivable asset-backed securities (ABS) are not subject to contraction risk since the underlying pool of loans is most likely:
explanation_en: Covered bond redemption regimes If fund sponsor defaults: Hard bullet Default triggered; payments accelerate Soft bullet Default delayed; final maturity date extended Conditional pass- Pass-through mode triggered only if bonds are not retired at through original maturity date A type of asset-backed security (ABS), a covered bond is secured by collateral consisting of a pool of loans (eg, auto loans, home mortgages). Interest and principal payments on ABS depend exclusively on the timely payment of the interest and principal on the underlying loans. Unlike other ABS, covered bonds offer an additional layer of protection since bondholders have dual recourse, which allows a claim on both the issuer and the cover pool (ie, underlying pool of loans). Other kinds of ABS are typically issued by a special purpose entity so that the issuer remains bankruptcy remote. If payments on covered bonds are not received as scheduled, stipulations in the issuing documents (ie, loan covenants) called redemption regimes determine how the bonds are impacted. The three types of covered bond redemption regimes are as follows: Hard bullet: Bond default is triggered and all payments are due immediately. This is the typical treatment for bonds of all types in the event of issuer default (Choice B). Soft bullet: Bond default is delayed and payments continue on the original schedule. The issuer's failure to pay does not trigger default since the maturity date is extended (eg, to 12 months). A failure to pay principal and interest on the new, extended maturity date will trigger default. Conditional pass-through: Bond default is not triggered and payments continue on the original schedule. If payments are not fully satisfied at maturity (ie, conditional), the bond is converted to pass-through mode, in which payments are funneled directly from the underlying pool to bondholders until the original expected cash flow payments are met (Choice C).

question_en: If covered bondholders do not receive payments as scheduled and the bond has a soft-bullet redemption regime, the bond default is most likely:
option_a: delayed, and final maturity is extended.
option_b: triggered, and bond payments are accelerated.
option_c: delayed, and the bond converts to a pass-through structure.
explanation_en: Asset-backed securities are bonds created from securitizing cash-generating assets, such as residential mortgages or credit card receivables. As the schematic above shows, the assets are bundled and sold to a special purpose entity (SPE) that uses them as collateral for bonds. The cash flows from the loans pay the bonds' interest and principal. Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) are a type of ABS. One type of risk that RMBS present to bondholders is default risk. This refers to the possibility that borrowers of the loans serving as collateral default, either in full or in part. Since the cash flows from the collateral are the primary source of payments for the bonds, defaults can significantly impact the bondholders' expected returns. Some securitization structures attempt to mitigate the risk of defaults through credit tranching. Instead of issuing only one class of bonds from the securitization, a credit-tranched structure uses multiple classes. Subordinate classes are the first to absorb losses caused by defaults in the collateral, which shields senior classes from some default risk. (Choices B and C) Extension risk and contraction risk are two types of prepayment risks. Securitizations may offer different classes of bonds that allow investors to determine how much prepayment risk they want to be exposed to; this is known as time tranching.

question_en: A mortgage-backed securities (MBS) issuer is concerned that interest rates will soon fall, so it structures tranches with various maturities to mitigate prepayment risk. This most likely describes:
explanation_en: Collateral for asset-backed securities (ABS) ABS Typical collateral Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) Residential mortgage loans Collateralized mortgage obligations (CMO) Mortgage-related products (eg, RMBS) Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) Commercial mortgage loans Collateralized debt obligations (CDO) Loans, other ABS, structured securities Non-mortgage asset-backed securities (ABS) Credit card loans, auto loans Securitized debt instruments, broadly known as asset-backed securities (ABS), are created using collateral which is sold to a special purpose entity (SPE). The SPE then sells bonds backed by the collateral. As shown in the table above, there are different types of ABS, which have different forms of collateral. Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) are bonds that are securitized by pools of residential mortgage loans. Agency RMBS are issued and typically guaranteed by a sovereign government or one of its agencies. A nonagency RMBS is issued by a private entity and has no government guarantee. The collateral for agency and nonagency RMBS consists of residential mortgage loans (Choice B). Credit card receivables, which are unsecured loans, are the collateral for credit card ABS (Choice A). A collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO) is similar to a residential mortgage-backed security except that the collateral is one or more ABS instead of actual loans. A typical CMO is structured with multiple tranches of bonds. Payments on the loans that secure the ABS are then distributed to the CMO investors. A sequential-pay CMO is designed so that each tranche is retired in order of seniority; only the most senior tranche then existing receives principal payments until that tranche has been retired.

question_en: In securitizations that create residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS), credit tranching most likely refers to multiple classes of bonds that offer unequal:
explanation_en: Bond credit enhancements and uses Enhancement Use Subordination Senior tranches have priority over junior tranches Internal Overcollateralization Issuer pledges assets worth more than the amount borrowed Reserve accounts Excess cash received from financed asset deposited in a separate account Surety bonds Payment guarantees issued by insurance companies External Letters of credit Guarantees from financial institutions other than insurance companies Cash collateral accounts Cash deposited by guarantor that issuer can borrow The process of securitizing pooled assets provides investors the opportunity to invest in tailored risk exposures and specified rates of returns. Investors' exposure to credit risk is reduced with enhancements, or features designed to redistribute risk by absorbing or reallocating potential losses. A common feature is credit tranching, in which pooled assets are segmented into tranches and each tranche is issued as a separate security, representing a different priority claim on the security's cash flows. Losses are allocated to tranches in a predetermined manner, with lower-rated tranches absorbing losses first. This structure is primarily used to shield investors in more senior tranches from default risk. It is also known as a waterfall structure due to how payments are allocated across tranches. (Choice B) Time tranching, not credit tranching, is primarily used to mitigate prepayment risk since it relies on segmenting the asset pool by using securities with different maturities. (Choice C) Overcollateralization may be used in addition to credit tranching. Generally, absorbed losses need to first exhaust the full amount of overcollateralization before the credit tranching structure applies.

question_en: A key distinction regarding collateral of a covered bond compared to other types of asset-backed securities is:
option_b: a covered bond's collateral remains on the issuer's balance sheet.
option_c: the issuer of a covered bond does not substitute for defaulted collateral.
explanation_en:
Covered bonds vs. other asset-backed securities (ABS)
Covered bonds Other ABS
Assets transferred to special entity
Assets remain on issuer's balance sheet
Investors exposed to credit risk if collateral
Issuer replaces nonperforming collateral
defaults
A covered bond is a type of asset-backed security (ABS) secured by collateral consisting of pools of loans (eg, auto loans, home mortgages).
Interest and principal payments on an ABS depend on timely payment of the interest and principal on the underlying loans. If the underlying loans
default, the ABS investors risk not receiving interest and principal.
Most ABS issues have a general structure in which the collateral is transferred to a special-purpose entity that becomes the security's legal issuer.
Bond indentures (ie, contracts governing the rights and obligations of the issuer and bondholders) typically allow bondholders to seek payment
from the special entity if the ABS defaults. This can limit recovery since, in most cases, the special entity has no assets other than the ABS
collateral.
Covered bonds mitigate bondholders' risk in two ways (ie, dual recourse). First, collateral remains on the issuer's balance sheet instead of
being transferred to a special entity; this gives investors in a covered bond direct recourse against the issuer. Second, if the covered bond's
collateral is in default, the issuer must replace it with good collateral; this replacement feature is not commonly used in other types of ABS.
(Choice A) Overcollateralization is an internal credit enhancement in which the issuer pledges collateral worth more than the bond's principal. It
can be used with all types of bonds, not just covered bonds.
(Choice C) Covered bonds do use collateral substitution to protect bondholders against losses from collateral default.

question_en: The pass-through rate for a mortgage pass-through security most likely refers to the:
option_b: monthly prepayment rate on the underlying loans.
option_c: weighted average coupon rate of the underlying mortgage loans.
explanation_en: A mortgage pass-through security (pass-through) is a bond created from bundling (ie, pooling) individual mortgage loans that serve as the collateral for the pass-throughs. The pass-through rate is the coupon rate for this security. Cash generated by payments on the mortgage loans is used to pay the pass-through rate as well as the security's principal. The collateral may consist of thousands of individual mortgages, and each might have a unique interest rate. The average interest rate for the collateral is referred to as the weighted average coupon (WAC). The pass-through rate is lower than the WAC since each pass-through has servicing and administrative fees (Choice C). In the diagram, the collateral's WAC is assumed to be 5.0%, while the pass-through rate is 4.5%. The 0.5% difference represents the servicing and administrative fees associated with the issue. (Choice B) The monthly prepayment rate is referred to as the single monthly mortality rate (SMM).

subtopic: 7.19 Mortgage-Backed Security (MBS) Instrument and Market Features
question_en:
An issuer constructs a mortgage pass-through security with the following underlying collateral:

| Mortgage | Remaining balance ($ thousands) | Mortgage rates (%) | Months of maturity remaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 80 | 4.5 | 48 |
| B | 100 | 5.0 | 60 |
| C | 120 | 4.7 | 72 |

If the issuer charges a servicing fee of 25 basis points, then the pass-through rate is closest to:
explanation_en: Issuers create mortgage pass-through securities (ie, pass-throughs) by pooling individual mortgage loans and using the pool as collateral for the pass-through security, which is then sold to investors. Investors receive cash returns generated from the pool of monthly mortgage payments. The mortgage pool usually consists of multiple mortgages with different interest rates. The pass-through rate (ie, coupon rate that pass-through investors receive) equals the weighted average coupon (WAC) less servicing and administrative fees. The WAC is the weighted average of the mortgage rates for the pooled mortgages, with the weights being each mortgage balance as a percentage of the total balances. In this scenario, the WAC is 4.75% and the fees are 0.25%, so the pass-through rate is 4.50%. (Choice A) 4.48% results from taking the simple average, not the weighted average, of the coupons. (Choice C) 4.75% results from not subtracting the servicing fee from the WAC.

question_en: The risk to the cash flows investors receive from agency pass-through mortgage-backed securities is most likely related to:
explanation_en: Prepayment risk of mortgage-backed securities Causes Consequences Effects on investment value Declining interest Shorter average life of mortgage- Higher cash flows in early years that must be Contraction risk rates backed securities reinvested at lower interest rates Defers more of cash flows to later years, Longer average life of mortgage- Extension risk Rising interest rates reducing their present value and price of backed securities security Agency pass-throughs are a type of mortgage-backed security (MBS): Investors receive a share of the interest and principal from a pool of mortgage loans. Since most mortgages give borrowers the right to prepay their loans, actual periodic cash flows from an MBS may vary as the effective maturity (ie, average life) of the MBS varies. Prepayment risk refers to the uncertainty of MBS cash flows and maturity. There are two components of prepayment risk: Contraction risk: Declining interest rates encourage borrowers to refinance their loans, resulting in early repayment (ie, prepayment) of the original mortgages. This accelerated return of principal forces reinvestment of higher-than-anticipated cash flows at lower interest rates. Extension risk: Rising interest rates cause fewer refinancings and prepayments, so a larger portion of MBS cash flows is deferred further into the future. The deferral of cash flows, along with the higher rates at which they are discounted, results in a decline in MBS values. (Choice B) Reinvestment risk relates to the uncertainty of the interest rate at which cash flows are reinvested, not the uncertainty of the cash flows received from holding an MBS. Changes in prepayment rates result in changes in the amount of reinvestment risk MBS holders are exposed to, so there is a connection between prepayment risk and reinvestment risk. However, they are defined as distinct types of risk. (Choice C) An agency MBS has either a government guarantee or an agency guarantee, so borrower defaults do not affect the cash flow uncertainty of these securities.

question_en: A portfolio of government securities is constructed to match the cash flow stream of the interest and principal payments of a commercial mortgage and to effectively retire that mortgage. This process is best described as a:
explanation_en: Defeasance Purpose A form of call protection for investors in commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) Occurrence When a borrower prepays a mortgage loan that is held in a CMBS The borrower must provide funds to construct a portfolio of government securities to match the original loan's cash flow Description stream Function To protect the CMBS investor from prepayment risk Unlike residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS), commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) use call protections to mitigate prepayment risk. Due to this call protection, CMBS trade more like corporate bonds than RMBS. Defeasance is a form of call protection for CMBS bondholders. To prepay a commercial mortgage loan in the underlying CMBS, a borrower must provide funds for constructing a portfolio of government securities to match the cash flow stream of the original interest and principal payments. This process effectively retires the loan—which has been defeased by the economically equivalent government securities portfolio— and the CMBS investor is made whole. (Choice B) A sinking fund arrangement details a schedule for gradually retiring a portion of a bond's principal over time. (Choice C) Securitization is the process of bundling cash-generating loans that serve as collateral for bonds.

question_en: For a commercial mortgage loan, a high debt service coverage ratio coupled with a low loan-to-value ratio is most likely indicative of:
explanation_en: Ratios for assessing credit risk Loan-to-value (LTV) = Loan amount / Property value Debt service coverage (DSC) = Net operating income / Annual principal and interest Commercial mortgage–backed securities (CMBS) consist of bundled commercial mortgage loans. Each loan is secured by income-generating commercial property that the lender may sell if the borrower defaults. Lenders should appropriately gauge each borrower's level of credit risk with metrics such as the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio and the debt service coverage (DSC) ratio. The LTV is the ratio of the loan amount to the property value. Low LTVs suggest that the borrower has a lower chance of defaulting due to high equity (ie, property value − loan amount). Furthermore, higher property value (denominator) relative to the loan amount (numerator) suggests that even if the borrower defaults, the lender can adequately recoup the loan with the proceeds from selling the property. The DSC ratio is the ratio of net operating income (NOI) to annual principal and interest owed, where NOI equals annual rental income less cash operating expense and depreciation reserve. High DSC ratios indicate that the borrower can better service its annual debt obligations, lowering credit risk. Therefore, a low LTV in conjunction with a high DSC confirms low credit risk. (Choice B) Balloon risk is primarily driven by the features of the mortgage, not the financial performance of the borrower; therefore, it is not indicative of credit risk. Balloon risk stems from underlying mortgages that require a disproportionally large principal repayment at maturity. (Choice C) Prepayment risk is primarily driven by the level of interest rates, not the financial performance of the borrower; therefore, it is not indicative of credit risk.

question_en: For commercial mortgage–backed securities, which of the following mechanisms is least likely to provide call protection at the loan level?
explanation_en: CMBS call protection mechanisms at the loan level Prepayment Disallows prepayments within a specified timeframe lockout Prepayment Predetermined percentage fee charged on outstanding penalty points balance if borrower wishes to refinance Yield maintenance Fee to compensate lenders based on the difference between charge new, lower borrowing rates and existing borrowing rates Borrower provides funds to the servicer to construct a portfolio Defeasance of government securities that replicates monthly mortgage payments CMBS = commercial mortgage–backed security. A commercial mortgage–backed security (CMBS) is created from pooled mortgages on commercial properties (eg, office buildings, warehouses). CMBS investors receive cash flows from the underlying commercial mortgage payments. Excess principal prepayments can arise as borrowers refinance existing loans when interest rates fall, which forces investors to reinvest the proceeds at a lower rate. A CMBS can limit prepayment risk for investors by providing call protection at the individual loan level and at the structural level. At the individual loan level, mechanisms such as prepayment lockout and yield maintenance charges discourage borrowers from making excess prepayments (Choices A and C). Yield maintenance charges compensate lenders and are based on the difference between new, lower borrowing rates and existing borrowing rates. At the structural level, certain mechanisms can redistribute aggregate prepayment risk from one class of investor to another. For example, sequential-pay tranches shift prepayment risk away from investors in one tranche by first distributing excess principal prepayments to other tranches.

question_en: A homeowner borrowed $850,000 in a 30-year fully amortizing recourse mortgage loan to purchase a house that secures the loan. The borrower defaults on the loan at the end of Year 3, when the loan has been amortized by $25,000. Interest rates have increased so that the present value of the loan is $800,000. If the lender forecloses on the loan and receives $750,000 from the sale of the house, the amount that the lender can recover from the borrower is closest to:
explanation_en: A mortgage is a loan for which specific real property is used as security. If the borrower defaults, the lender can foreclose on the collateral, which means that the lender can seize the property and sell it to repay the loan. A recourse loan means that the lender can seize other assets from the borrower if the proceeds are insufficient to fully repay the loan. In a nonrecourse loan, the collateral is the lender's only source of repayment. In this question, the outstanding loan amount is $825,000 ($850,000 − 25,000) when the borrower defaults. The sale of the collateral results in proceeds of $750,000, so $75,000 remains unpaid on the loan balance. The question stipulates that this is a recourse loan, so the lender can assert a claim for $75,000 against the borrower's additional assets. (Choice A) $50,000 is the difference between the proceeds from the sale of the collateral and the present value of the loan. Shortfalls from foreclosures are based on the amortized loan balance, not the present value of the loan. (Choice C) $100,000 results from incorrectly calculating the outstanding balance as $850,000; this fails to account for the $25,000 amortization.

question_en: Which of the following best describes a consequence of a nonrecourse mortgage loan in the event of default?
option_a: The borrower cannot be forced into foreclosure.
option_b: The borrower can be held liable for the entire loan balance.
option_c: The lender receives only the proceeds from the sale of the property.
explanation_en: Residential mortgage default remedies Borrower is responsible for the entire mortgage balance Recourse loan Lender has a claim on borrower's other assets to satisfy any shortfall Common in European countries Lender receives only the proceeds from the sale of the property Nonrecourse loan Borrowers often turn to strategic default on underwater mortgages Common in the United States A residential mortgage is a loan with residential property used as collateral. If the borrower defaults, the lender can foreclose, which is a legal process by which the lender can take possession of the property and sell it to obtain payment for the loan. Recourse and nonrecourse refer to the legal options available to a lender in the event that the borrower does not pay the scheduled interest and principal payments. In a nonrecourse loan, the lender can claim only the proceeds from the sale of the property. In a recourse loan, the lender can seize other assets from the borrower if the proceeds from selling the property are insufficient to fully repay the loan (Choice B). (Choice A) Foreclosure is a remedy for the lender in the event of a default under either loan type.

question_en: An issuer creates a sequential-pay collateralized mortgage obligation that consists of Tranches A, B, C, and D. The face value of each tranche is paid in order of seniority, with Tranche A the most senior and Tranche D the least senior. The collateral consists of 30-year residential mortgages. An investor in Tranche D most likely assumes a greater exposure to:
explanation_en: A collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO) is a type of mortgage-backed security (MBS). A CMO has multiple issues, or tranches, of bonds that are backed by the mortgages. The cash from mortgage payments pays bonds' interest and principal. Each tranche has different rules regarding both the timing and amount of principal that it receives from the collateral's cash flows. In a sequential-pay residential CMO, all tranches receive interest payments but only the most senior tranche (Tranche A in this example) receives principal (including any prepayments) until its face value has been paid. The next senior tranche (Tranche B) then receives principal, and so on, until all tranches have been paid. Junior tranches (eg, Tranche D) must wait until the tranches senior to them (eg, Tranches A, B, and C) are completely paid. This increases the extension risk (ie, the risk that the maturity will be longer than expected) to junior tranches. (Choice A) Balloon risk is a type of default risk that applies to CMOs that are backed by commercial mortgages. Many commercial mortgages require a large principal payment at maturity (ie, the "balloon"). CMO investors are exposed to the risk that the borrower will be unable to make the balloon payment. (Choice C) Contraction risk is the possibility that the bond will mature more quickly than anticipated due to higher-than-expected prepayments. This risk is more associated with senior tranches of a sequential pay CMO.

question_en: Which of the following types of residential mortgage loan is least likely to result in a balloon payment at maturity?
explanation_en: An amortizing loan is characterized by a payment schedule that gradually increases principal repayments over time. In a traditional fixed-rate mortgage loan, the total payment is fixed, but over time the underlying principal component increases while the interest component decreases. Fully amortizing loans completely pay both principal and interest by the time the last scheduled payment is made. Thus, the mortgage loan has been fully satisfied, and the borrower is under no additional obligation. (Choice A) Interest-only loans do not include any principal payments. At the end of the mortgage period, the entire original principal balance is due as a balloon payment. (Choice C) Partially amortizing loans do not completely retire the principal, resulting in a balloon payment, which is the remaining principal needed to retire the loan. Balloon payments often require the borrower to refinance the remaining principal into a new mortgage loan.

question_en: A local bank advertises the availability of 30-year home mortgages that carry a 4% annual interest rate for the first 10 years. After that, the interest rate becomes variable until maturity. This type of mortgage is most likely a:
explanation_en: A mortgage is a loan that is collateralized by specific real property, such as a house. Payment of interest and principal on mortgages can be structured in different ways. A hybrid mortgage begins as a fixed-rate mortgage for a specified period (eg, 10 years). At the end of the period, the mortgage automatically changes to a variable rate mortgage for the remainder of its life. (Choice B) A variable mortgage has a variable interest rate from inception until it matures. (Choice C) A convertible mortgage is similar to a hybrid mortgage, except that the borrower decides whether the mortgage becomes a variable rate at the end of the initial fixed-rate period.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a credit enhancement for commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS)?
explanation_en: Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) typically include multiple bond classes (ie, tranches), each with its own credit rating. CMBS allocate cash flows and credit losses from the underlying collateral to create a series of senior and subordinate tranches and offer investors a range of credit ratings and credit risk. CMBS use subordination as a credit enhancement to allocate collateral losses to the lowest-rated (ie, most-subordinated) tranche with remaining principal value. The more junior (ie, more subordinated) the tranche, the greater the exposure to credit risk. The more senior the tranche, the greater the protection from credit losses and the lower the tranche's credit risk. (Choice B) Call protection at either the structural level or the loan level protects investors from prepayment risk and therefore is not a credit enhancement. (Choice C) The loan-to-value (LTV) ratio is a loan-level credit risk evaluation tool. Limits to the LTV ratio may reduce the credit risk of the underlying loans that form the collateral for the CMBS, but they do not impact the credit losses allocated to CMBS tranches as a credit enhancement would.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a difference between mortgage pass-through securities and collateralized mortgage obligations (CMOs)?
explanation_en: Issuers create pass-through securities (ie, pass-throughs) by pooling mortgage loans that serve collectively as an underlying cash-generating asset and as collateral. Investors can purchase shares of a pass-through security and receive the pass-through rate. Since there is only one class of pass-through shares, all investors receive the same percentage returns and are exposed to the same level of prepayment risk (Choice C). In contrast to pass-throughs, collateralized mortgage obligations (CMOs) offer multiple security classes (ie, tranches). Different tranches are tailored to different investor risk preferences. In sequential-pay CMOs, as shown above, investors who can tolerate more extension risk (ie, longer maturity than expected) may invest in subordinate tranches that offer higher returns in exchange for higher risk. (Choice B) CMOs distribute prepayment risk across tranches but do not eliminate it.
